note: Landau's theorem is about generalized Dirichlet series Σ a_n e^{-λ_n s} whose coefficients are eventually positive. Its conclusion is that the real point of the line of convergence is a singularity. The Lean is about Laplace integrals of a function g. Landau needs a one-sided sign condition for all large n. The Lean needs only an averaged upper bound on windows [U,(1+δ)U] for a sequence of U → ∞, which is a strictly weaker hypothesis. To get the Lean's conclusion (no pole with Re ρ > θ) from a Landau-type theorem, apply it to K e^{(θ+ε)u} − g. Real poles with positive residue and complex poles are excluded by different arguments, and the Lean's pole hypotheses are built for this. Landau states none of this. The method is the same: expand in a Taylor series at a real point to the right and use positivity of the coefficients (p. 537, eq. (15)). The upstream proof does the same with the Taylor coefficients of Φ at σ > 2.

note: The source allows K any complete discretely valued field of mixed characteristic (0, p) with perfect residue field; the Lean takes K a finite extension of Q_l inside a fixed algebraic closure (a special case). The source states one equivalence of categories T : Vect^φ(Spf(O_K)_Δ, O_Δ) → Rep^crys_{Z_p}(G_K). The Lean splits it into essential surjectivity (clause 1) and full faithfulness (clause 2), and replaces the functor T by a relation 'E is realised by (T, ρ, j)', i.e. an A_inf-semilinear map E(A_inf) → W(C♭) ⊗ T inducing the Artin–Schreier isomorphism E(A_inf) ⊗ W(C♭) ≅ T ⊗ W(C♭), compatible with Frobenius and G_K. This is how the source describes T(E) in §5 (construction after Theorem 5.2, p. 14: T = (M ⊗_{A_inf} W(C♭))^{φ=1} with M ⊗ W(C♭) ≃ T ⊗ W(C♭)), but the identification of the two formulations is not itself stated as a theorem. The source's F-crystals are vector bundles on the ringed site (X_Δ, O_Δ) with an isomorphism (φ*E)[1/I_Δ] ≃ E[1/I_Δ] (Definition 4.1). The Lean encodes them as compatible finite projective modules on all bounded prisms with base-change transition maps, and the Frobenius as a family of isomorphisms after inverting each single element d ∈ I, tied together by a compatibility condition; prisms are classically (rather than derived) (l, I)-adically complete. These are encodings a reader should check against Definition 4.1; they are not the source's wording. Clause 2 of the Lean quantifies over arbitrary Z_l-modules T, T' and arbitrary maps ρ, ρ' : G_K → End(T) that occur in some realisation, rather than over the étale realisations T(E), T(E') themselves; the source's full faithfulness is about Hom(E, E') → Hom_{G_K}(T(E), T(E')). Clause 1 of the Lean defines 'crystalline' through an abstract period-ring package (P, AI) together with the hypothesis IsStd that it is isomorphic to the standard B_cris and B_dR; the source uses Fontaine's B_crys directly.

citation.title: $p$-adic Hodge theory and values of zeta functions of modular forms

note: The Lean is a consequence of Kato 14.2(1) rather than a literal instance. Take Kato's f to be the Lean's newform (k = 2e+1), r = e, and Kato's abelian field K to be the Lean's imaginary quadratic K. Since k is odd, 1 ≤ e ≤ k-1 and e ≠ k/2 hold automatically. By (14.10.3) on printed p. 240, det(1 - Fr_ℓ^{-1}u) = 1 - a_ℓ u + ε(ℓ)ℓ^{k-1}u^2 with Fr_ℓ the arithmetic Frobenius. That is the Lean's Att convention, so W(-e) ≅ V_{F_λ}(f) ⊗ Qbar_l and W ≅ V_{F_λ}(f)(e). Two facts make the semisimple W(-e) isomorphic to Kato's V: Brauer–Nesbitt with Chebotarev, and the irreducibility of V_{F_λ}(f) (Ribet 1977). Neither is stated in the linked theorem. Kato proves that the discrete Selmer group Sel(K,T) ⊂ H^1(K, T⊗Q/Z) is finite. The Lean states that the rational group H^1_f vanishes. The rational statement follows by a standard argument that the source does not state. The image of H^1_f(K, V(e)) in Sel(K,T) is divisible of corank dim H^1_f(K, V(e)), so finiteness forces H^1_f(K, V(e)) = 0. Restriction then embeds H^1_f(Q, W) and H^1_f(Q, W⊗θ) into H^1_f(K, W), because H^1_f(K, W) = H^1_f(Q, W) ⊕ H^1_f(Q, W⊗θ) with θ the character of K/Q. The Lean thus packages the χ = 1 and χ = θ parts of Kato's statement over K. Kato's theorem needs only that f is a newform, any l (including 2), any abelian K and any non-central critical r. The Lean's hypotheses are much stronger and are not used by Kato. They are Used (l odd, l ∤ disc(K)h_K, (l-1) ∤ 2e, residual reducibility, ordinarity at l, level conditions, irreducibility over K(μ_{l^∞})) and WitAQ (automorphy/local-global compatibility over CM quadratic fields). So the Lean is a special case in its hypotheses. The Lean works with coefficients in Qbar_l, with continuous cocycles valued in Qbar_l^2 (Z1 requires continuity), and with a Selmer condition imposed at one chosen place above each prime. Its crystalline condition uses the project's ring Bcr (UpperTheory.V.Loc.Bcr = (PP l).R.B), not checked to be Fontaine's B_cris. There is no condition at archimedean places, which is harmless for l odd. Kato's Sel(K,T) (14.1) uses Bloch–Kato's H^1_f with F_λ-coefficients over all places of K. Base change from F_λ to Qbar_l and the agreement of the local conditions are assumed, not checked against the project's definitions. Kato's theorem also gives Sel(K,T) = 0 for almost all λ, and 14.2(2) treats the central twist. The Lean uses neither.
